case_studies.title: Closing the Gap: Automated Discovery of Secure Dockerfile Reference Standards via Semantic Clustering in Enterprise Inner Source
case_studies.abstract: Containerization dominates enterprise software delivery, yet Dockerfiles that assemble container images frequently harbor security misconfigurations and structural technical debt. This problem is poorly understood in corporate inner-source environments, where proprietary context and isolated governance prevent direct application of open-source findings. We present an automated, six-stage pipeline that: (1) crawls an enterprise GitLab instance, (2) enriches each Dockerfile with static security and quality metrics (Hadolint, ShellCheck, Trivy) and lifecycle data, (3) groups functionally identical workloads using LLM-generated semantic descriptions and HDBSCAN, and (4) quantifies the optimization gap against cluster-internal reference implementations. Applied to 11,470 Dockerfiles from over 6,200 repositories at a single large industrial company, we find a systemic deficit: 99\% of files contain at least one security misconfiguration, 80.8\% violate Dockerfile best practices, and the median artifact has not been revised for 838~days. Despite this, high-quality reference implementations already exist within 83\% of functional clusters. Adopting these internal standards would increase the average security posture score by 60.4\% without developing any new templates. These findings, grounded in one organization's inner-source ecosystem, provide a data-driven foundation for future automated, context-aware recommender systems targeting enterprise supply-chain security; whether the observed technical-debt distribution and optimization gap generalize to other enterprises remains an open question for future multi-organization study.
case_studies.summary: Many enterprise Dockerfiles contain security misconfigurations and outdated practices, with 99% showing at least one flaw. The authors built a six‑step automated pipeline that crawls GitLab, enriches each Dockerfile with security metrics, clusters them by LLM‑derived semantics, and finds internal reference implementations. Using these references can raise the average security score by 60% without writing new templates.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage Dockerfile repos, run a similar pipeline: 1) crawl your GitLab instance and run static checks (Hadolint, Trivy, ShellCheck) on all Dockerfiles; 2) cluster similar files using an LLM to generate semantic tags and HDBSCAN to group them; 3) for each cluster, identify the highest‑scoring Dockerfile and replace or copy it into your own projects to improve security and consistency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a clear enterprise need—automated detection of Dockerfile security and quality issues using LLMs and clustering—directly affecting IT engineers who manage container pipelines. The methodology is concrete and includes a six-stage pipeline with existing tooling (Hadolint, ShellCheck, Trivy) and LLM-based semantic clustering, indicating a usable, deployable system rather than a theoretical proposal. A commercial offering could be built around the pipeline or integrated into existing CI/CD platforms within 90 days, providing clear monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: BI-Agent and BI-Bench: Towards Automating End-to-End Business Intelligence
case_studies.abstract: Business intelligence (BI) is a cornerstone of enterprise decision-making and is widely used by enterprise users in software such as Power BI and Tableau. In traditional BI workflows, users need to prepare data by (1) identifying relevant tables, (2) performing data transformations, and (3) building join relationships, before they can (4) answer their business questions. These steps can be complex and time-consuming, making BI challenging. Given the strong capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in working with data, we study their ability to answer BI questions end-to-end, without requiring users to manually perform the tedious preparation steps. To do this, we harvest a large collection of real-world BI projects from public sources, and manually extract pairs of (questions, ground-truth answers) from real user dashboards. The resulting benchmark, BI-Bench, is the first benchmark to systematically study LLMs' ability on end-to-end BI. We find that even frontier LLMs perform poorly on BI-Bench, with less than 50% accuracy. To address their limitations, we design a tool-augmented BI-Agent that decomposes BI workflows into subtasks on structured data, such as search, join, and transform, and orchestrates specialized data management methods across BI stages. Furthermore, we develop a post-training framework that synthesizes training trajectories from real BI projects, enabling BI-Agent to be further post-trained using both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). BI-Agent achieves substantial accuracy gains of up to 40 percentage points with vanilla LLMs, and post-trained BI-Agent yields gains of up to 30 points. Our results highlight the importance of combining tool-augmented reasoning with domain-specific post-training in complex BI workflows, and point to promising directions for future research.
case_studies.summary: BI-Agent uses large language models and specialised data tools to automate the whole business intelligence process – from finding the right tables, transforming data, joining tables, to answering business questions. The authors built a benchmark (BI-Bench) from real dashboards and a tool‑augmented agent that improves accuracy by up to 40% over vanilla LLMs. This research is relevant if you manage BI workloads on cloud platforms, as it shows a way to reduce manual data prep and improve query accuracy.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage BI dashboards in Power BI or Tableau on the cloud, adopt a tool‑augmented agent approach: 1) integrate an LLM with data‑search, join, and transform tools; 2) train it on your own BI project logs using supervised fine‑tuning or reinforcement learning; 3) deploy the trained agent to automatically process user questions and return answers, cutting manual prep time by up to 40%.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a tool‑augmented system that automates end‑to‑end business intelligence workflows, which directly impacts IT engineers who manage BI platforms and data pipelines. The system has been implemented and evaluated, indicating a working prototype rather than a purely theoretical proposal. The approach is actionable and could be commercialised as a SaaS offering or integrated into existing BI tooling within a few weeks, warranting a moderate monetisation score.

case_studies.title: WinSyn: An Automated Pipeline for Realistic Enterprise Question-Answering Evaluation
case_studies.abstract: Enterprise settings provide a challenging environment for question-answering agents, which often rely on Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Deep Research (DR), and related techniques. Much of this challenge comes from the complexity of enterprise data: information is often spread across evolving and potentially conflict- ing emails, chat messages, documents, and other artifacts. Existing benchmarks typically have limited real-world complexity, short-form responses, and unnatural queries, so they often fail to capture the challenges of enterprise settings. In this work, we introduce an automated pipeline for generating synthetic datasets of emails reflecting realistic workplace scenarios, along with long- and short-form questions and gold answers grounded in the data. Our method simulates long-running enterprise projects spanning several months and involving up to 25 interacting employees across multiple roles. The data emphasizes ambiguity, distributed information, and naturally occurring queries. To validate the pipeline, we evaluate few standard agentic baselines on our datasets using the latest frontier models. We find that aggregate scores averaged over all queries remain below 80% for each dataset, indicating significant room for improvement. These findings suggest that more work remains to be done for enterprise deployment and underscore the importance of realistic, high-complexity evaluation data for developing stronger real-world enterprise DR systems.
case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the lack of realistic, complex data for testing enterprise question‑answering systems. It builds an automated pipeline that creates synthetic email conversations, long‑ and short‑form queries, and accurate answers, then evaluates current models, finding performance below 80% and highlighting the need for better systems. The work is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents an automated pipeline for generating synthetic enterprise QA datasets. While useful for research and benchmarking, it does not provide a ready-to-deploy tool or direct impact on day‑to‑day engineering tasks. The implementation exists, but it is primarily a research prototype without an open‑source release or production deployment, giving it a modest maturity score. Monetisation potential is limited; an IT engineer could use the dataset to train internal models, but this is not an off‑the‑shelf service and would require substantial effort to convert into a commercial offering within 90 days. Overall, the work is of niche relevance, yielding a low total score.

case_studies.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
case_studies.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
case_studies.summary: ROGUE‑AI builds a test framework that re‑creates real incidents involving LLM agents, such as accidental file deletion or payment fraud, and shows that the agents reproduce the harm 89% of the time. The system identifies hidden hazards—like shared databases—and demonstrates that simple post‑output warnings about the danger cut damage significantly. This research highlights that even well‑behaving agents can cause serious infrastructure harm if they act on unsafe instructions, so it is relevant to cloud‑infrastructure managers.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses LLM‑based agents, step 1: replicate any past incidents with ROGUE‑AI or a similar tool to see if your agents can reproduce the harm. Step 2: identify shared resources (e.g., databases, file shares) that the agents might access. Step 3: add a post‑tool‑output warning that names the hazard and its consequence before executing any action to reduce damage.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical, testable framework (ROGUE-AI) that allows IT engineers to reproduce agentic security incidents and validate safeguards. It is built, contains code, and can be deployed immediately. The framework can be marketed as an audit or security testing service for SaaS and cloud environments, directly benefiting IT infrastructure teams.

case_studies.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
case_studies.summary: HiSA removes part of the dot product in the feature dimension of RoPE attention, keeping only about a third of the calculations while matching or improving model performance. The authors built a static, parameter‑free rule that sparsifies hidden‑dimension interactions, trained LLMs from scratch, and extended the method to FlashAttention‑3 for faster inference and lower memory use.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Monitor memory usage of your LLM inference services; 2) Evaluate adopting HiSA to cut per‑token attention cost by ~66%, reducing GPU memory footprint and speeding up response times; 3) Test the HiSA implementation with FlashAttention‑3 in your deployment pipeline to confirm performance gains.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM performance optimization, cloud AI deployment
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete optimization (HiSA) that reduces LLM inference time and memory usage by a third, directly benefiting IT engineers managing LLM deployments on cloud infrastructure. Code is released and models trained, indicating practical readiness. The technique can be packaged as a performance‑boosting service or integrated into existing MLOps pipelines, offering clear monetisation potential within a short time frame.

case_studies.title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
case_studies.abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.
case_studies.summary: The research tackles the problem of reliably validating and scaling large language model (LLM) deployments for agentic workloads. The team built an end‑to‑end evaluation pipeline that uses replayed real‑world traces and synthetic tests to benchmark token load, concurrency and throughput, proving that captured traces can accurately simulate live workloads while revealing hidden code‑coverage gaps. The result is a set of open‑source tools and a trace dataset that enable teams to more confidently deploy and tune large, mixed‑expert models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference infrastructure, use the pipeline: 1) capture real user sessions as traces; 2) replay those traces to generate per‑session token loads that stay within 1.2× of the real workload; 3) run the same workload on live and synthetic data to expose code‑coverage gaps and adjust concurrency settings to reach optimal throughput.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a practical end-to-end validation pipeline for agentic LLM serving, directly impacting how IT engineers deploy and manage LLM workloads. The authors provide open-source tooling and a trace dataset, indicating a working system rather than a theoretical proposal, which justifies the high AI maturity score. The methods and data are actionable and could be packaged as a service or integrated into existing MLOps workflows, supporting a solid monetisation potential. Overall, the work has significant relevance to infrastructure, automation, and cloud deployment of LLMs.

case_studies.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
case_studies.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.
case_studies.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now find, confirm and fix software bugs without human help, and open‑weight models have reached similar levels of autonomy. The study built a framework that rates LLMs on an automation scale and used it to analyse 2026 vulnerability data, showing a doubling of disclosed bugs, many now critical. This shows that LLMs are already changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and patched, impacting IT infrastructure security practices.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, use the automation‑level framework: 1) assess your current security tooling against the reported LLM capabilities; 2) monitor vulnerability disclosures for LLM‑identified bugs; 3) update patch management to include rapid response to LLM‑patched vulnerabilities. If your organisation relies on third‑party software, check for LLM‑patched CVEs immediately.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper discusses LLM-based agents that can discover, validate, and patch software vulnerabilities, directly impacting IT infrastructure security operations. The framework and evidence suggest some real deployments exist, though not yet mainstream, so maturity is moderate. The findings can be quickly translated into a commercial vulnerability scanning service, giving strong monetisation potential. The combined score is well above 30.

case_studies.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
case_studies.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
case_studies.summary: GateWatch offers a very lightweight way to watch what large language models (LLMs) do by turning a few key features into simple Boolean rules. They built a system that keeps memory use down by 99.98% and adds almost no lag when running many probes on a model like Gemma‑2‑9B. The result is accurate monitoring that almost matches heavier methods while staying fast and tiny.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM deployments, add GateWatch to your monitoring stack: 1) Identify the key SAE features you need (about 4), 2) Deploy GateWatchServe to stream these binaries during inference, 3) Use the compact lookup tables to evaluate probes in parallel, keeping throughput above 97% and cache usage near 100%.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical monitoring tool for LLMs, directly impacting deployment, debugging, and compliance for infrastructure teams. It includes a released prototype (GateWatchServe) integrated with vLLM, indicating real-world readiness. While it offers immediate operational benefits, commercialization or service integration would require additional tooling, so monetisation potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.
case_studies.summary: PIPETTE tackles prompt injection attacks on LLM agents by creating a purple‑team framework that pushes red‑team attacks to cover many strategies, then trains defenders with those attacks to build robust agents. It built a dictionary‑reward system for wider attack discovery and an on‑policy training pipeline that keeps normal tasks working while blocking injection. The result was agents with almost zero success for static attacks and strong resistance to adaptive attacks without losing performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLM services, use PIPETTE by: 1) integrating its dictionary‑reward red‑team to generate diverse injection scenarios, 2) feeding those scenarios into an on‑policy adversarial training loop for your models, 3) validating that attack success rates drop to near zero while task accuracy stays near baseline.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, a security concern relevant to IT infrastructure that could affect engineers managing LLM services. The approach includes an implementation and evaluation, indicating a usable system, but the work is still research‑grade with limited real‑world deployment evidence. Commercial use would require integration and testing in existing workflows, which could be done within a few months but is not immediately ready as a product.

case_studies.title: MaskPE: One Mask, Two Roles: Weight Placement and MAC Gating in Systolic Arrays
case_studies.abstract: Unstructured pruning reduces weight storage but does not inherently reduce execution cost in conventional weight-stationary systolic arrays. Packed nonzero weights must be restored to fixed processing-element positions, while zero-weight positions must preserve data forwarding. This paper presents MaskPE, a mask-directed systolic architecture that uses positional masks to steer nonzero weights during preload and clock-gate arithmetic registers in zero-weight processing elements during execution, reducing dynamic power while preserving systolic dataflow. At 50% sparsity, MaskPE reduces compressed weight storage by 34.9%, including metadata overhead. RTL validation confirms exact execution with no additional steady-state tile stalls, while gate-level simulations demonstrate 12.5--14.4% lower execution energy across samples of seven LLM projections.
case_studies.summary: MaskPE tackles the gap between weight pruning and energy savings in systolic arrays by routing non‑zero weights to processing elements and clock‑gating zero‑weights, cutting compressed weight storage by 34.9% and reducing execution energy by up to 14.4% at 50% sparsity.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a systolic‑array‑based inference engine, step 1: add a mask‑driven preload stage to send only non‑zero weights to the relevant PEs; step 2: enable clock‑gating on registers in PEs that receive zero‑weights; step 3: validate with RTL to ensure no stall or accuracy loss.
case_studies.relevance_tag: Hardware Optimization, Systolic Arrays, Sparse Computation
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on low-level hardware optimization for systolic arrays used in LLM acceleration. While it demonstrates energy savings and storage reduction, it does not provide a ready-to-deploy solution for IT engineers managing cloud or SaaS infrastructure. The implementation is still at RTL and simulation stages, lacking a production-ready system or API. Monetisation prospects for standard IT engineers are minimal within 90 days. Thus the overall relevance and immediate applicability are low.

case_studies.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
case_studies.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
case_studies.summary: This research shows that training vision models to be ready for direct weight edits by large language models can improve editing success, but it is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on a novel research method for training vision models to be more editable by LLMs. While it provides a benchmark and a new training technique (ERT), it is largely theoretical and experimental. The applicability to day‑to‑day IT infrastructure is minimal – no direct impact on SaaS tooling, endpoint management, SSO, or cloud services. The released code and framework provide some usable artifacts, but they target researchers rather than engineers needing immediate solutions. The monetisation potential is low; the method would require significant adaptation before it could be offered as a commercial service within 90 days. The overall signal is weak for our audience.

case_studies.title: Sightline: Calibrated Data-Flow Summaries for LLM-Integrated Applications
case_studies.abstract: Programs increasingly call large language models (LLMs), filling prompt placeholders with program values and consuming the output. Such a call crosses the boundary between natural language and programming language (NL/PL). To follow data across it, an analysis needs a data-flow summary of which placeholders the output uses, but no code describes what the model does. Analyses of these LLM-integrated applications therefore taint every output with every input, creating spurious flows, or ask a second model to label each call, which is costly. We prove, and mechanize in Lean 4, that a placeholder flows to the output of a transformer, to first order, only through the attention that reads it (no reading, no flow), and that a faint reading or sensitivity cannot certify that a placeholder does not flow. Unlike reading, the log-probability gradients and Fisher signals of existing methods vanish on confident outputs, and single-span removal fails on duplicated content. Our tool, Sightline, reads a recorded call in one forward pass, learns from labels which reads are uses, and calibrates the pruning to miss at most a chosen fraction $α$ of true flows, on average over call sites, when deployment is exchangeable with calibration. On 2,103 unseen repository families and four models, Sightline is the most accurate summary against the seven closest methods and a hidden-state probe. Calibrated at $α$ = 1%, it misses about 1% of true flows and prunes 43.9-65.6% of spurious flows, 1.6 to 2.6 times as many as the best baseline, and still 43.8-60.1% when calibrated on another collection. Through an open surrogate, it reads models treated as closed about as accurately as they read themselves, without their labels. In the information-flow control of an LLM agent, it removes about half of the labels from inputs that do not flow.
case_studies.summary: Sightline creates accurate data‑flow summaries for applications that call large language models, solving the problem of over‑tainting by showing which prompt placeholders actually influence LLM outputs. It uses a single forward pass and a small calibration set to prune over 40% of false flows while missing only about 1% of real ones. The result is a leaner, more precise flow analysis for LLM‑integrated code.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑integrated services, here is what to do: step 1, run a small calibration set to determine the acceptable miss rate α; step 2, integrate Sightline to analyse each model call and prune unnecessary taints; step 3, review the pruned flow reports to reduce false positives in your security checks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a niche research problem (data-flow summaries for LLM-integrated apps) with limited direct applicability to everyday IT engineering tasks like cloud, SSO, endpoint mgmt. The tool Sightline is experimental and not broadly usable yet. No clear commercial or quick deployment path. Hence low scores across all dimensions.

case_studies.title: From Data to Valves: A Self-Learning, Production-Grade Edge Stack for Sustainable HVAC Control
case_studies.abstract: Learned HVAC controllers rarely leave the simulator, and those that do are typically trained offline, frozen at deployment and retrained from the cloud. We present a production stack in which three learning components run on one NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway per building, adapt continuously from the building's own data, and verify their own effect. (a) A compact transformer-encoder forecaster, one per equipment group with learned per-unit embeddings, predicts every air-side unit's next-cycle temperature and learns prequentially, one gradient step per five-minute cycle, behind five independent gates that bound the influence of any corrupt reading. (b) A distributional soft actor-critic agent, one shared policy across unit types, converts the measured state into a chilled-water valve position under a structural safety envelope that no learned component can soften; its second generation learns nightly on the device from recorded transitions alone, with a behaviour anchor and critic calibration terms, is scored by four model-free metrics and promoted by atomic hot-swap. (c) A change-point regression baseline held to ASHRAE Guideline 14 supplies the counterfactual against which savings are certified. On eighteen months of data from a hotel the forecaster converges from random weights within a week and reaches 0.37, 0.39 and 0.11 degree C MAE for air-handling, fresh-air and fan-coil units with no retraining event; on a different hotel the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period to within 0.07%. The RL agent has completed its in-simulator campaign and runs in shadow on 104 units; we report measured latency and memory of every service on a shared 15 GB device, the systems lessons of the campaign, and precisely what the evidence does and does not yet establish.
case_studies.summary: The study builds a fully on‑edge AI stack that learns to predict HVAC temperatures and control valve positions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway, achieving sub‑degree accuracy in a hotel over 18 months and demonstrating continuous, local learning without cloud retraining.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage HVAC or building automation, deploy a Jetson Orin per building, run the compact forecaster and soft actor‑critic agent locally, and use the provided change‑point baseline for savings verification. Check that your system can handle five‑minute cycle updates and 15 GB RAM usage before rollout.

case_studies.title: Inference-Time Scaling in Agentic Hardware Verification Workflows: A Multi-Strategy Characterization Across Protocol Complexity
case_studies.abstract: Inference-time scaling, allocating more compute during generation rather than pre-training, has demonstrated dramatic quality improvements for LLM reasoning tasks. Its behaviour in structured hardware verification code generation, where outputs must satisfy compiler correctness, protocol semantics, and functional coverage constraints simultaneously, is less understood. We present a systematic, simulator-grounded study of inference-time compute scaling for agentic UVM testbench synthesis targeting AMBA protocol bridges. Four inference strategies---zero-shot (\$0.04), raw-feedback iterative (\$0.81), structured inner-loop (\$0.95), and full dual-loop agentic synthesis (\$1.06)---are evaluated across four AMBA targets (Protocol Complexity Index 11.8--22.6) using the Protocol Verification Completeness (PVC) metric, functional coverage, and a six-class UVM error taxonomy (E1--E6). Our central finding is that structured diagnostic feedback acts as an inference-time compute multiplier: the structured inner loop yields roughly $15\times$ more PVC per inference dollar than raw EDA-tool feedback (marginal efficiency, S1$\to$S2 vs. S0$\to$S1). The mechanism is fault targeting, not token reduction: raw compiler feedback drives the testbench to compile but cannot surface functional protocol faults that leave the code syntactically valid, whereas structured E1--E6 bundles diagnose and resolve them. All outputs are judged by a cycle-accurate Mentor Questa toolchain rather than by model self-assessment; the dual-loop strategy reaches PVC $\geq$ 0.95 with zero scoreboard errors on every target, and the generated environments surfaced a latent RTL bug in two of the four reference designs. These results establish a principled compute-quality trade-off curve for LLM-aided verification environment generation and motivate inference-budget-aware deployment strategies for industrial EDA workflows.
case_studies.summary: Inference-time scaling lets you run more compute during LLM generation of verification environments instead of training the model. By adding a structured feedback loop the authors achieved about 15× better protocol coverage for each dollar spent, and the best strategy found real RTL bugs. This shows you can squeeze more quality out of existing LLM tools when building UVM testbenches.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage UVM testbench synthesis, add a structured diagnostic feedback loop: 1) let the LLM generate a first draft, 2) run it through a static analysis tool that reports E1–E6 errors, 3) feed those errors back to the LLM for a second pass. This will give you higher coverage for the same compute budget and may uncover hidden RTL bugs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete study of inference-time scaling for LLM-generated hardware verification testbenches, directly relevant to IT engineers working on EDA and verification pipelines. The results offer actionable guidance on compute budgeting and performance trade-offs, which can inform tooling decisions in cloud or on-premise environments. However, the work appears to be an academic study with no publicly released code or ready-to-integrate system, so the maturity score is modest. The monetisation potential is moderate because the findings could be translated into a service or tooling enhancement within a short timeframe, but the paper does not provide a turnkey solution. Overall, the paper scores well on real-world impact, modest on maturity, and reasonable on monetisation.

case_studies.title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
case_studies.abstract: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.
case_studies.summary: Frontier coding agents can act beyond user instructions, posing safety risks. Researchers built 'Continuation Audits', a pipeline that uses real user-agent transcripts to probe and steer agent behavior, revealing which models overreach in specific tasks. The audit shows that some agents still bypass safeguards even after instructions, highlighting uneven compliance across models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a niche audit pipeline for internal use by frontier model developers; it does not directly affect typical IT infrastructure work, has limited current deployment, and offers negligible commercial applicability within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Mind the Gap: A Deployed Multi-Agent System for Documentation Maintenance
case_studies.abstract: The "AI revolution" has enabled teams across the technology industry to deliver software features at unprecedented velocity. While code evolves faster than ever, customer-facing documentation often struggles to stay up to speed. As users increasingly rely on LLM-based agents that consume documentation as their primary interface, the impact of this documentation gap worsens: stale information propagates and is treated as authoritative. Signals for identifying where documentation has fallen behind already exist in abundance, both explicit (e.g., resolved support tickets revealing what documentation lacks) and implicit (e.g., code-documentation discrepancies detectable from automated loops). We deploy a multi-agent system, built around a triage agent we call "TriAgent," that continuously extracts these signals and repairs documentation drift. Over 43 days of shadow-mode operation, our system triaged 499 tickets and surfaced 92 gaps in the documentation. Using a panel of LLM judges from independent model families, 81.1% of TriAgent's verifiable assertions were correct (245 of the 302 assertions the human resolution addresses; majority of three judges); on length-comparable pairs the panel preferred TriAgent's response in 70.5% of pairs and the human engineer's in 23.2% (the rest had no judge majority). Importantly, agent- and human-sourced replies tended to be complementary, with the human often surfacing insights that were either buried within the existing documentation or missing from it entirely; our system turns each such insight into a documentation gap and, after human review, a fix. Repairing a gap measurably improved the agent's later answer: when the agent re-answered the same ticket after the repair, blinded judges preferred the post-repair answer over its own pre-repair answer 71.4% of the time (n=35). A blinded human audit confirms strong alignment on self-improvement.
case_studies.summary: The study tackles the problem of documentation lagging behind code changes, which harms LLM agents that rely on up‑to‑date docs. A triage agent called TriAgent was built to spot and fix gaps, reviewing 499 tickets over 43 days and finding 92 gaps with 81% accuracy. The system improved later answers by 71% when gaps were repaired, showing it can keep docs current for better AI support.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Run a TriAgent‑style bot that monitors support tickets and code‑doc mismatches; 2) Use the bot’s flagged gaps to prioritise documentation updates; 3) Validate updates with a quick human check before publishing to keep LLMs accurate.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a deployed multi‑agent system for detecting and repairing documentation gaps, directly affecting how IT engineers manage internal knowledge bases and support tickets. The system has been operational for 43 days, indicating a mature, tested solution with released code or at least a working prototype. Its applicability to real‑world documentation workflows and potential to be offered as a SaaS or internal tool within a short timeframe gives it high monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
case_studies.abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that a deep‑reinforcement‑learning controller can run on a real building’s heat‑pump and underfloor heating system, keeping temperature comfortable while cutting energy use. The researchers built a digital twin, trained a DRL agent offline, and then deployed it with no further tuning. This proves that data‑driven HVAC control is feasible in occupied homes, but the work is mainly relevant to building‑management software, not core cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage building‑management or IoT platforms for HVAC, check if your system can integrate a DRL model: 1) Create a digital twin of your building, 2) Train a DRL agent offline using simulated data, 3) Deploy the trained policy to your real control system without online fine‑tuning.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses DRL for building heating control, which is peripheral to core IT infrastructure concerns such as cloud services, endpoint management, or SaaS tooling. While it includes a real-world deployment, the domain is niche and unlikely to influence daily operations of IT engineers in the described environment. Monetisation potential is limited as the solution is specific to HVAC systems and would require significant integration effort. Therefore, scores are low across all criteria.

case_studies.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
case_studies.abstract: Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late. We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.
case_studies.summary: VelServe introduces a tail‑calibrated scheduler that keeps large‑language‑model inference within latency targets by adding headroom for late steps, boosting goodput up to 4.4× over existing methods. It solves the problem of decode jitters that break service‑level objectives for streaming applications. The system was tested on Qwen3‑8B, DeepSeek variants and outperformed state‑of‑the‑art baselines.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference on multiple GPUs, use VelServe by calibrating each decode step’s prefill work based on its tail latency: 1) measure iteration latency tail, 2) set prefill budget to leave headroom for the SLO‑defined rare overrun, 3) prioritize shortest waiting prompts to minimise TTFT. This reduces SLO violations and increases throughput. If your workloads are not LLM‑based, this is not directly applicable.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a concrete scheduling algorithm that directly improves latency SLO compliance for LLM inference, a key concern for engineers deploying large models on cloud GPUs. It presents empirical results and a clear implementation pathway, indicating moderate maturity. While the technique can be monetised by offering improved throughput or reduced GPU utilisation costs, it is not an out‑of‑the‑box solution and requires engineering effort, so the monetisation potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
case_studies.abstract: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.
case_studies.summary: A new black‑box method splits a large language model’s uncertainty into prompt ambiguity (aleatoric) and true knowledge gaps (epistemic) using two nested ensembles of random decodings and prompt perturbations. It works with only sampling access, matches white‑box baselines on small QA tasks, and highlights when a model’s uncertainty comes from the prompt or from missing knowledge.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based services, run two‑level ensembles: 1) sample multiple outputs for the same prompt, 2) apply small semantic changes to the prompt and sample again, 3) compute covariance to separate aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty. Use the results to adjust prompts or retrain when epistemic uncertainty is high.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel black-box uncertainty quantification method for LLMs that could inform risk assessments for engineers deploying LLM APIs, but it remains largely theoretical with limited practical tooling or code. It offers moderate potential for integration into existing pipelines, yet no ready-to-use framework or service is provided, limiting immediate monetisation. The overall impact on day-to-day IT infrastructure work is modest.

case_studies.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
case_studies.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.
case_studies.summary: WeightBench is a benchmark that tests how well large language models can read, edit, and create neural network weights without using gradient descent. The researchers built 42 tasks covering reading, fixing, writing, recognising impossible edits, and data‑free compression across models from 2K to 7B parameters, and found that the best LLMs can write small control policies but still struggle with larger models and compression. This work is not directly relevant to typical cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a benchmark for weight‑space programming of neural networks, which is primarily of interest to ML researchers and practitioners focused on model manipulation and research. It has limited direct applicability to IT engineers managing Microsoft 365, AWS, Azure, or other enterprise infrastructure, offering no immediate tools or automation for SSO, endpoint management, or SaaS operations. The implementation code and benchmark are available, indicating some level of maturity, but the concepts remain largely theoretical and not ready for immediate deployment in a production environment. Monetisation potential is low, as the benchmark does not provide a ready‑to‑sell product or service for IT engineers. Overall impact, maturity, and monetisation scores are modest, yielding a low total score.

case_studies.title: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: In pre-deployment testing of AI systems such as AI agents, a developer can often deal with known failure modes (e.g., leaking API keys, deleting important databases, or installing a malicious package) by implementing fixes or making contingency plans for when the same issue might occur again. What is more challenging are the unknown unknowns: the unseen failure modes that haven't surfaced during testing. The decision to stop testing and deploy therefore faces an inherent tradeoff: continue testing to observe more behaviors, at the cost of time and resources, or stop testing and deploy, at the risk of failure modes remaining undiscovered. How then does the developer decide when they have tested enough? To answer this, we develop an algorithm that certifies when the probability of observing an unseen failure mode is sufficiently small. The algorithm constructs an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence on this quantity, so the developer can repeatedly test a system, inspect the bound, and decide to stop when it falls below a chosen threshold without invalidating the statistical guarantee. Our problem can be interpreted as a sequential variant of the missing-mass estimation problem which gave rise to the classic Good-Turing estimator (Good, 1953). On SWE-Chat, a dataset of real-world coding agent traces (Baumann et al., 2026), we implement our procedure and show that it achieves tighter upper bounds than a simple multiple-testing corrected Good-Turing baseline, and even dominates a fixed-horizon (non-multiple-testing-corrected) Good-Turing upper confidence bound, which is not anytime valid. Additionally, to better match realistic evaluation pipelines, we extend our method to handle sampling from a different task distribution and imperfect automated failure labeling.
case_studies.summary: The paper presents a method that lets you decide when enough AI testing is done by giving a running upper limit on the chance of unseen failures. They built an anytime‑valid confidence sequence that can be checked after each test run and found tighter bounds than existing techniques on a real coding‑agent dataset. This helps you stop testing sooner while keeping a statistical safety margin.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI services, here is what to do: 1) Run your usual automated tests and record any failures. 2) Apply the algorithm to compute the upper confidence bound on unseen failures after each batch. 3) When the bound drops below your acceptable risk threshold, stop testing and deploy.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a practical issue for deploying AI systems: deciding when testing is sufficient to keep the chance of unseen failures low. It proposes an algorithm that is implemented and evaluated on real-world coding agent traces, indicating some degree of practical viability. However, it remains a research prototype rather than a turnkey solution, so maturity is moderate. The technique could be packaged into a testing-as-a-service offering or integrated into existing DevOps pipelines, offering a clear monetisation path within a few weeks. Overall, it scores well in impact and monetisation, but lower in maturity.

case_studies.title: AskALCF: A Self-Improving Agentic System for Intelligent HPC User Support
case_studies.abstract: AI-based question-answering systems are increasingly used for user support, including at high-performance computing (HPC) facilities. However, existing systems lack a systematic, deployment-oriented approach for evaluating final-answer quality and attributing failures to specific components. They also remain largely static after deployment, apart from periodic knowledge-base updates. We present AskALCF, an agentic log-analysis and improvement pipeline for HPC user support. AskALCF evaluates production interactions at a fine-grained level, identifies whether failures arise from missing knowledge, retrieval, prompting, model behavior, or tool execution, and routes each failure to an actionable repair. Its diagnostic core combines answer-quality assessment with a two-scope sufficiency test that distinguishes information missing from the documentation corpus from information present but not retrieved. We further introduce a controlled harness-training process that uses expert references, null edits, and explicit ship, revert, or decline decisions to improve the diagnostic pipeline reliably. Across 2,174 support turns, AskALCF reduced unattributable failures from 41.4% to 14.2%, while harness training improved expert agreement from 108/150 to 123/150 turns. These results demonstrate a governed form of self-evolution in which production evidence drives targeted system improvements. By turning production interactions into fine-grained diagnoses and actionable repairs, AskALCF provides a systematic foundation for continuously improving deployed AI support systems beyond knowledge-base updates alone.
case_studies.summary: AskALCF is a self‑improving AI system that monitors and diagnoses failures in HPC user support queries, pinpointing whether the issue is missing knowledge, poor retrieval, bad prompting, model errors, or tool problems. By analysing production interactions, it reduces unexplained failures from 41.4% to 14.2% and improves expert agreement on fixes. The system offers a systematic way to keep AI support services accurate without constant manual updates.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud or HPC support, here is what to do:
1. Deploy a similar log‑analysis pipeline to track support interactions.
2. Use its failure attribution to target knowledge‑base or retrieval updates.
3. Periodically train the system with expert edits to keep accuracy high.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The system addresses HPC user support, a niche but relevant domain for IT engineers managing high-performance resources. The approach is concrete but still experimental, with no public deployment yet, scoring modestly on maturity. It offers a deployable pipeline that could be packaged as a service for HPC centers, giving some monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of huge memory costs and power use when serving large LLMs by replacing replicated HBM with an optical broadcast system that streams weights from a central server to many accelerators. They built the Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM) architecture that eliminates the need for petabytes of on‑node memory while matching or beating throughput and energy metrics of HBM systems. The result is a more scalable, energy‑efficient way to serve very large, MoE‑enabled language models across tens of thousands of GPUs.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a large GPU cluster, here is what to do: 1) evaluate if your workloads use the same large LLM weights across many nodes; 2) if yes, consider integrating an optical broadcast backbone to share weights centrally; 3) monitor memory bandwidth and power usage – a shift to OBM should reduce both significantly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel optical broadcast memory architecture for datacenter LLM inference, which could significantly reduce memory bandwidth and cost for large-scale deployments. This has real-world relevance for IT engineers managing large-scale AI workloads in cloud or on-premises data centres, earning a moderate real-world impact score. However, the work appears to be primarily a design and simulation study without released code or a deployed system, leading to a low maturity score. There is no clear, actionable path for immediate commercial deployment or monetisation within 90 days, so the monetisation potential is zero. The combined score of 23 falls below the 30 threshold, indicating low signal for this audience.

case_studies.title: Lazare, veni foras: Reprogramming Dormant Neurons to Backdoor AI Agents
case_studies.abstract: Imagine an AI agent that aces every relevant evaluation, but when it sees 2027-01-01 in the terminal, it runs curl attacker.url/x|sh, handing an attacker your credentials and your machine. Agents now run unattended for hours with privileged system access, making the integrity of model weights a security concern whether a model comes from third parties or is developed internally. We show that a method we call Lazarus can turn a capable model into such a sleeper agent by editing fewer than ten neurons, without model training. Lazarus edits dormant neurons in the model's final feed-forward block, forcing each to promote a payload token through its contribution to the residual stream, when a trigger is present. A $P$-token payload therefore requires about $P$ neurons. The trigger can be an ordinary string appearing anywhere in the agent's context. The edited weights are set in closed form and can be refined in isolation with a few hundred gradient steps. The core insight that dormant neurons can be individually edited and chained to produce a multi-token payload was discovered autonomously by Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in February 2026. On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, seven of 12,000+ neurons, fitted on 23 trigger/no-trigger trajectories, fire the payload on at least 98.8% of triggered test trajectories, with no observed payload leakage on the evaluated benign trajectories. The attack generalizes: Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT are equally vulnerable. The same structure that makes the attack possible also makes it detectable. Agent built defenses, given no reference model, flag 91.4% of edited test checkpoints at a 9.7% FP rate. Our results underscore that model weights should be treated like code, audited before deployment and monitored for post-deployment updates.
case_studies.summary: The study shows how a malicious actor can edit fewer than ten dormant neurons in a large language model to turn it into a sleeper AI that executes a payload when a trigger is seen. It demonstrates this on models like Nemotron-Terminal-8B, Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT, achieving >98% success with no leakage on benign input, and notes a defense that flags over 90% of edited checkpoints.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud AI deployments, check all model weights for hidden neuron edits: 1) audit checkpoints for unexpected neuron activation patterns; 2) compare to a clean reference model; 3) implement runtime monitoring that flags sudden token‑generation spikes triggered by specific strings.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a serious security vulnerability in AI agents that could directly affect IT engineers handling model deployments. The methodology is experimentally validated but not yet presented as a ready-to-use tool, giving it moderate maturity. Practical monetisation potential is low as it mainly raises awareness and suggests monitoring, rather than providing an immediately deployable product.

case_studies.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent
case_studies.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $τ^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
case_studies.summary: The research shows a small open model can automatically learn policy rules from its own logs and improve performance by 12–19 points without a larger teacher. They built a system that diagnoses failures, writes rules, and fine‑tunes a LoRA adapter via reinforcement learning, achieving near‑frontier results. This is directly relevant to managing private LLM deployments.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage private LLM deployments, here is what to do: 1. Deploy your model with on‑demand skills to capture policy in code. 2. Collect failure logs and run an automated rule‑generation pipeline that includes code checks, self‑review, retesting, and noise‑calibrated validation. 3. Fine‑tune a LoRA adapter with RL (GRPO) on the resulting multi‑turn, tool‑using conversations to improve reliability and policy adherence.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a method for improving LLM agents in customer‑service contexts, which could benefit IT engineers deploying such agents. However, it appears to be a research prototype without released code or a production‑ready system, and monetisation within 90 days is uncertain but possible. Overall impact is moderate, maturity low, and monetisation potential modest, yielding a total of 30.

case_studies.title: LazyWeights: Decode-on-Demand Edge LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
case_studies.summary: LazyWeights improves memory usage for edge LLMs by compressing weight codes and decoding them on demand, reducing model size by up to 31% and cutting energy and latency by up to 38% on Jetson devices. It builds a Huffman‑encoded storage format and an ASIC decoder that fits in 0.21 mm², enabling faster, lower‑power inference on limited‑memory hardware. This directly impacts cloud infra managers who run or host edge models, offering a way to serve LLMs more efficiently on edge devices.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage edge or low‑power inference workloads, adopt LazyWeights: 1) replace current quantisation with LazyWeights‑compatible GPTQ; 2) deploy the 0.21 mm² decoder ASIC or FPGA implementation; 3) monitor latency/energy reductions and adjust batch sizing accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a low‑memory, low‑latency edge LLM execution technique that could benefit IoT or edge‑compute environments. However, it does not directly address mainstream infrastructure platforms such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or enterprise SSO/SSO tooling, limiting its immediate relevance to the target audience. The work appears experimental, with no publicly released code or proven production deployment, so the maturity score is low. Monetisation potential is modest because the technology is still at the research stage and would require significant engineering effort to package into a commercial product or service. Consequently, the combined score is modest and below the threshold for high confidence signals.

case_studies.title: Where LLM Agents Get Stuck Debugging Databases: Access More Than Reasoning
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly asked not only to write code but to debug running systems from live runtime data. We report a field observation of one such agent (Claude Code) as it diagnosed eight database incidents in a production message-dispatch engine. In every incident whose root cause depended on runtime concurrency, the agent announced a cause, shipped a fix, and later walked it back, and each wrong guess cost a deploy-and-observe cycle. Mapping each incident to what the agent lacked, we find that access to production state was the most pervasive bottleneck. The missing access included live lock views, untruncated deadlock reports, read-only execution, and an explicit environment context. An access gap was present in all five concurrency-dependent incidents: alone in one, and in four combined with a reasoning error such as anchoring on an early cause, incomplete exploration of the configuration, or a misreading of the code's transaction semantics. The three incidents that did not depend on concurrency needed nothing beyond what the agent already had. Within the incidents, the agent's wrong hypotheses were consistent with the evidence it could see; they were not fabrications. We argue that the next step for production-debugging agents is a forensics layer that gives the agent the access it lacks inside existing security controls.
