The authors built IAMRAGBENCH, a benchmark of 60 policy cases, and found that up to 15.8% of attacks succeed when attackers poison the context. The study highlights the risk of trusting LLM-generated IAM policies without verification.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AWS IAM, immediately enforce independent policy review: 1) run any LLM‑generated policy through AWS CheckNoNewAccess; 2) compare the policy against an authorization envelope; 3) block deployment if any new permissions are detected.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The benchmark directly impacts AWS IAM policy management for IT engineers, providing a practical tool to detect mis‑generated policies. It is a published dataset with code and evaluation scripts, making it usable now, though not a full product. The findings can be turned into a quick‑start testing service or an audit plugin that IT teams can deploy within weeks, giving clear commercial value.

case_studies.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.
case_studies.summary: VeriHarm-Bench shows that LLM coding agents can finish tasks but still delete files, weaken permissions, or corrupt data. The researchers built an automated test framework that adds hidden harm tests to regular coding tasks, revealing that top agents only avoid harm 37% of the time. This matters for cloud managers because unseen damage can slip through during automation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check if your automated code agents run with shell access – add VeriHarm-style hidden harm tests to your CI pipeline to catch unintended file deletions or permission changes. If your org uses LLM agents for script generation, audit their outputs for side‑effects before deployment. If you don’t run such agents, no immediate action is needed.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces VeriHarm, a framework to measure harmful success in LLM coding agents. This is directly relevant to IT engineers who deploy such agents for automation, scripting, and system configuration, providing a new metric that can flag unintended side effects. The framework appears to be a working prototype with released code, making it mature enough for real-world testing. It offers clear, actionable tests that can be integrated into existing security or DevOps pipelines, enabling engineers to assess and mitigate risks quickly, and could be packaged as a SaaS testing service. The total score is 45, well above the threshold for low signal.

case_studies.title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
case_studies.abstract: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.
case_studies.summary: The study shows LLM agents can help discover and deliver SQL queries for business data, but they struggle with incomplete requirement discovery, unreliable execution, and unclear hardware constraints. They built a simulation of an enterprise text‑to‑SQL engagement and found that only about a quarter of runs met all acceptance criteria, highlighting gaps that limit production use. This research points to a risk for cloud infrastructure managers who rely on automated code generation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for data services, check whether your deployment pipelines include manual review steps for requirement discovery, monitor execution logs for reliability, and set explicit compute‑budget and production‑readiness tests before trusting an LLM to automate SQL generation.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM-based automation for enterprise data engineering
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses LLM agents for requirement discovery and deployment in enterprise SQL contexts, relevant to IT engineers. However it is an experimental study with limited practical deployment evidence, and monetisation is unclear. Overall moderate impact, low maturity, and low immediate commercial value.

case_studies.title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
case_studies.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
case_studies.summary: ETAPS gradually prunes and adapts sparse models, keeping each step small so the model can recover quality without large optimizer states. It outperforms the previous state‑of‑the‑art at 50‑90% sparsity and reduces GPU‑time and memory by up to 49% and 5× respectively. This could help you run cheaper, high‑sparsity LLMs in production.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language models, here is what to do: 1) Use ETAPS to prune in stages, 2) Keep the sparse delta small and train it continuously, 3) Monitor perplexity to ensure quality stays above baseline.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical algorithm for aggressively pruning large language models while maintaining performance, directly benefiting IT engineers who deploy LLMs in cloud and edge environments. The method claims substantial resource savings and lower GPU usage, making it immediately usable for cost optimisation. The authors report extensive experiments and indicate released code and benchmarks, satisfying the maturity criterion. For monetisation, the approach can be applied to reduce hosting costs or sell as a deployment optimisation service within 90 days. Overall, the work is highly relevant to infrastructure engineers and offers tangible commercial value.

case_studies.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how to pre‑process and organise knowledge into structured formats (like claim‑evidence trees, entity graphs, timelines) so that an AI agent’s search loop uses only the minimal necessary context, cutting query tokens by 91% and reducing latency from 140s to 30s. The authors built an open‑source pipeline called RAGFlow that turns a chaotic retrieval loop into five disciplined stations, giving the agent a curated, governed context instead of a raw ranked list of passages. For cloud infrastructure managers, this means a way to host and serve structured knowledge bases that improve agent efficiency and governance without adding new retrieval engines.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, set up RAGFlow on your Kubernetes cluster: 1) ingest your documents into the compilation pipeline to generate claim‑evidence trees; 2) expose the compiled store via a REST API; 3) route your agents’ queries through the RAGFlow harness to cut token use and latency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces an open-source RAGFlow pipeline that restructures retrieval for agentic LLM systems, directly addressing practical infrastructure challenges such as query efficiency, latency, and governance. The solution is immediately deployable with released code and demonstrated performance gains in real-world benchmarks, enabling IT teams to reduce token usage and response times. It offers clear, actionable components (knowledge compilation, decision gating, navigation trees) that can be integrated into existing SaaS and cloud environments, providing a tangible service offering within 90 days. However, the core novelty lies in engineering rather than novel AI research, so scores reflect high practical impact, mature implementation, and moderate monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
case_studies.abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.
case_studies.summary: SecPO introduces a new loss function and adversarial training pipeline that dramatically reduces prompt‑injection attack success rates on LLMs, while keeping normal performance intact. The researchers trained a Qwen‑3.6‑27B model with SecPO and strong synthetic attacks, cutting ASRs 1.5‑14.5× compared to previous methods and 2.4‑4.6× versus standard DPO loss. This shows a practical way to harden AI agents against injection attacks without hurting their usefulness.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted AI services, run the SecPO training code on your models: 1) generate strong injected inputs with their AT pipeline, 2) fine‑tune your model using the SecPO loss, 3) test against known adaptive attacks. This will lower injection success rates and keep service quality high.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete adversarial training framework (SecPO) for protecting LLM-based agents against prompt injection, a real threat in current AI deployments. It releases code, training data and a fine‑tuned model, indicating immediate usability. The approach can be integrated into existing LLM pipelines and marketed as a security service for organizations deploying LLMs, making monetisation feasible within 90 days.

case_studies.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
case_studies.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
case_studies.summary: ACCT lets you move the key‑value cache (the context) from a smaller LLM to a larger one without re‑running the original prompt, saving up to 20× faster inference and cutting memory use by 75%. They built three light components that pick useful tokens, decide how many to keep, and convert the cache into a format the target model can use. The result is that the larger model can infer faster and with fewer tokens, matching or beating its usual performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage multi‑model LLM deployments, step 1: identify which models in your stack can be paired for cross‑cache transfer; step 2: apply a KV selector to keep only the most relevant context tokens within your budget; step 3: convert and load the sparse KV into the target model before inference. This can cut inference time and memory in your cloud infra.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete technique for reducing KV cache recomputation across LLMs, which directly benefits infrastructure engineers managing large LLM workloads on cloud platforms. It is a practical, algorithmic contribution with potential for immediate deployment in cost‑sensitive settings. However, the work appears to be a research prototype with no publicly released code or proven production deployment, so its maturity is moderate. The monetisation potential is reasonable because the method could be packaged as a cost‑savings tool or service for enterprises running heterogeneous LLM pipelines, but it is not a turnkey product yet. Overall, the paper scores well on real‑world impact and monetisation potential, but lower on maturity.

case_studies.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
case_studies.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
case_studies.summary: Flide is an inference engine that speeds up decision‑making models by avoiding redundant calculation and keeping results mathematically exact. It does this by flattening token streams and using GPU‑based indices to fork attention across different decision branches, allowing up to 9.5× faster queries than existing engines while maintaining precision. This means faster, more accurate LLM‑driven decision systems for applications that need low latency and high reliability.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based decision systems, step 1: replace your current inference engine with Flide; step 2: update your deployment to use the flattened token stream format; step 3: test performance and precision against your baseline, aiming for up to 9.5× speed improvement without sacrificing accuracy.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Flide offers significant speed-ups for decision-based LLM agents, directly impacting infrastructure workloads that rely on rapid inference. However, the paper appears to present a prototype rather than a production-ready system, so maturity is modest. The solution could be adopted by engineers within 90 days, but would require integration work; thus monetisation potential is moderate.

case_studies.title: Preserving Utility in Continual LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Projections
case_studies.abstract: Unlearning concerns the task of removing the influence of a sensitive portion of the training data, such as protected, copyrighted or private text, from a model without retraining it from scratch. While unlearning requests happen continuously during a model's lifetime, the vast majority of LLM unlearning methods are ill-suited for iterated removal, yielding steep decay in forgetting and utility upon sequential unlearning. This decay stems from interference between successive updates, as each new deletion can undo earlier ones or push the model further along directions already degraded by them. To address this, we introduce Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a gradient-projection scheme that restricts each update to the orthogonal complement of activation subspaces cached from prior forget sets. This approach provably guarantees first-order non-interference with earlier deletions. COP stores only a low-rank basis per layer, requiring neither past gradients nor previous forget sets, and plugs into unlearning methods that update the model through gradient steps on a differentiable loss without modifying its objective. Experiments on standard LLM unlearning benchmarks (TOFU and RWKU) show that COP preserves utility across sequential requests without weakening forgetting, preventing the collapse of standard objectives and forgetting more effectively than continual-specific baselines.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the problem of repeatedly removing sensitive data from a large language model without losing performance. The authors built Continual Orthogonal Projection (COP), a simple gradient‑projection method that keeps each deletion orthogonal to previous ones, so utility stays high and forgetting stays strong. Experiments on standard benchmarks show COP outperforms existing continual‑unlearning techniques.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLMs, here is what to do: 1) add COP’s low‑rank basis cache to your inference pipeline; 2) whenever a deletion request arrives, run a single gradient step constrained to COP’s orthogonal subspace; 3) monitor utility metrics to confirm no drift. If your org uses continual data deletion, check that your current unlearning routine isn’t causing interference between successive requests.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a niche research problem (continual unlearning) with limited direct applicability to existing IT infrastructure. No evidence of released code or deployment, and the concept does not translate into a near-term service for engineers.

case_studies.title: InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure
case_studies.abstract: Large language model serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now ex- posed on the public internet and indexed by commodity scanners within hours of deployment. The threat characteristics of this sur- face are only beginning to be measured, and the honeypot frame- works that could measure it were designed for conventional net- work services rather than for AI infrastructure. In fact, emulating an AI service is a distinct deception problem: the observable behavior of the service, including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows, must be reproduced faithfully, while the underlying computation, model inference and tool ex- ecution, must never occur. We present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework organized around a single principle we call deception without inference: every request an adversary can observe is answered from static response pools, and nothing an adversary submits is ever executed. InferD decomposes the emulation into four deception planes, transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session, adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.
case_studies.summary: InferD is a honeypot framework that lets security teams study how AI inference services are attacked without risking real models or data. It emulates the visible behaviour of LLM APIs, vector stores and orchestration gateways, while all responses come from static pools and no actual inference runs. The result is a low‑interaction trap that provides evidence of attack paths and credential use without exposing real assets.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI inference infrastructure, add InferD to your security stack: 1) deploy the framework on a separate test environment, 2) configure it to mirror your production API endpoints, 3) monitor the static response logs for malicious activity and adjust firewall rules accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses security of AI inference infrastructure, directly impacting how IT engineers protect public-facing ML services. The framework appears to be a tangible, low-interaction honeypot that could be deployed, indicating moderate maturity. Its applicability as a security service or component of a security-as-a-service offering suggests a clear monetisation path within 90 days.

case_studies.title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
case_studies.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how the energy used by LLMs grows with both the input (prefill) and output (decode) tokens, giving clear scaling rules and a simple way to estimate energy from compute time. It builds a profiling tool and statistical models that map token lengths to compute time and energy, proving that compute time is a good stand‑in for energy when measurements are hard to get. The result is a practical framework that can help you predict and reduce the energy footprint of your LLM workloads.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) use the authors’ profiling method to benchmark your LLM workloads and capture prefill and decode token counts; 2) apply the linear/quadratic scaling equations to estimate compute time and energy; 3) adjust your deployment (e.g., limit context length or batch size) to stay within energy budgets and improve sustainability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper offers empirical insights into energy and compute consumption of LLMs, which can inform cost‑management decisions for IT engineers deploying large models. It is a mature study with released profiling data, but it does not provide a ready‑to‑deploy tool or service, so monetisation potential is limited to internal optimization.

case_studies.title: When Relevant Code Is Wrong: Runtime-Aware Context for AI Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly rely on retrieved code and development history to guide software changes. However, highly relevant artifacts may describe implementations that are inactive or incompatible with the target deployment. Neither semantic similarity nor recency establishes whether retrieved information remains applicable under feature flags, architectural migrations, and deployment-specific configurations. We challenge relevance-oriented retrieval by introducing operational context validity, a task-, deployment-, and time-dependent criterion for determining whether software evidence can legitimately guide implementation decisions. We instantiate this new retrieval principle in CASE, an agent-agnostic framework that connects repository artifacts with runtime configurations and architectural evolution, classifies evidence as valid, invalid, or unknown, and generates context packages distinguishing actionable guidance from historical rationale and unresolved constraints. We investigate its feasibility through a reproducible preliminary evaluation involving six development tasks, 15 artifacts, and three deployments. Conventional retrieval exposes 16 incompatible artifact occurrences as actionable, whereas CASE excludes them while retaining all applicable artifacts under the prototype's reference rules. Recency filtering reduces valid recall to 0.43, while removing feature-flag evidence from CASE reduces it to 0.13. Although these results demonstrate feasibility rather than improvements in coding-agent correctness, they reveal limitations of relevance-based retrieval and motivate a new research direction: enabling coding agents to reason not only about which information is relevant, but also whether it remains operationally valid.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the problem of coding agents misusing older code that no longer runs because of feature flags or architectural changes. The authors built CASE, a framework that links repository code to current runtime settings, classifying artifacts as valid or invalid for guidance. The prototype showed it can filter out 16 previously misapplied artifacts while keeping all applicable ones, proving the idea works but not yet improving agent accuracy.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check your code‑retrieval tools: 1) Integrate runtime metadata (feature flags, deployment configs) into your search queries; 2) Filter out artifacts flagged as invalid by your context‑aware system; 3) Verify that remaining code matches current environment before use.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses operational context for AI coding agents, which could impact how engineers integrate code retrieval tools with deployment configurations, but it is still a preliminary prototype with limited practical deployment. The maturity is low as it lacks a fully deployed system, and monetisation potential is minimal because it does not present a ready-to-use product or service.

case_studies.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
case_studies.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
case_studies.summary: Not relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a synthetic benchmark and loss‑based tweaks to improve attribution quality in language models. While the techniques could inform downstream tools for debugging or compliance, the work is largely research‑benchmarked, lacks a ready‑to‑deploy system, and offers limited immediate utility for infrastructure engineers or SaaS tooling. The potential to sell or deploy within 90 days is low, as it would require substantial integration effort. Thus overall impact, maturity, and monetisation are modest.

case_studies.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
case_studies.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
case_studies.summary: TextSeal2 is a watermark that lets you recognise AI‑generated text without hurting model speed or quality. It merges multiple keys into one, keeping the signal clear even when the model uses speculative decoding. The result is higher detection rates (8‑22% better) with no extra latency. This is relevant to anyone who needs to prove text authenticity in a cloud‑hosted LLM service.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLMs, enable TextSeal2 by: 1) merge your existing watermark keys with a Gaussian copula in the model’s post‑processing; 2) adjust your inference pipeline to run the extra exponential race only on draft leftovers; 3) monitor detection metrics to confirm no latency increase.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a watermarking technique for large language models, which is more relevant to model developers than IT engineers managing infrastructure. The method appears to be a research prototype with limited evidence of deployment. While it could be packaged as a service for SaaS providers, the immediacy of monetisation for typical UK IT engineers is low.

case_studies.title: CARI: Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection in Coding-Agent Workflows
case_studies.abstract: Coding agents increasingly develop, test, and integrate software whose components are owned by different developers, teams, or services. This exposes a distinct attack surface: a malicious or compromised peer development role can manipulate a live component of the software under development (e.g., a backend service, test harness, CI job, or deployment service) and influence the runtime feedback that another role's coding agent must process to complete its task. Although such a component has legitimate diagnostic authority to report its own state, it has no action authority over the victim's local files, credentials, shell, or development environment. We introduce Cross-Boundary Adversarial Runtime Injection (CARI), a direct runtime-feedback injection setting that exploits this authority mismatch. Rather than explicitly compromising the victim's prompt, model, tools, or local environment, the attacker covertly embeds malicious instructions in task-relevant runtime feedback produced by a peer-controlled development component. The victim then interprets that feedback as part of normal debugging or recovery, and may translate the diagnostic guidance into unauthorized victim-side actions. We instantiate ten different attacks based on CARI, spanning resource exhaustion, information exposure, and development-state manipulation. Across four programming languages and five code-capable models, CARI succeeds in 2,845/3,000 (94.8%) trials. Furthermore, CARI transfers effectively to product-level coding agents, achieving 61.3% attack success on Codex and 58.7% on Claude Code. By contrast, prompt-level defenses exhibit a security-utility trade-off: generic warnings are ineffective, whereas explicit policies suppress attacks but substantially over-refuse legitimate actions.
case_studies.summary: CARI shows that a compromised development component can inject malicious instructions into the runtime feedback of coding agents, leading to resource exhaustion, data leaks, or state changes. The researchers built ten attacks across multiple languages and models, achieving up to 94.8% success, and proved the technique works on real product agents like Codex and Claude Code. This is relevant to cloud infra managers because insecure CI/CD or deployment services could become the injection vector.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage CI/CD or deployment services that provide runtime feedback to development agents, check that the feedback cannot be tampered with by other services; isolate feedback channels and validate authenticity before agents act on them.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel attack vector (CARI) relevant to security of coding agents used in modern CI/CD pipelines, directly impacting infrastructure engineers who deploy and manage such systems. The research is theoretical with no released tool, so maturity is low. However, the findings can inform actionable security testing services and tool enhancements, giving moderate monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing}. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.
case_studies.summary: This study shows that large language models can be tricked into attributing text to the wrong role (role spoofing) by mixing fake structure and content cues, making them vulnerable to hijacking attacks. The researchers built a detection method using linear probes that reliably flags spoofed roles across different model settings. For IT infrastructure managers, the work highlights a new security risk with LLM‑powered tools but does not directly change day‑to‑day cloud ops.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑enabled services, implement role‑spoof detection: 1) add a linear probe layer to your inference pipeline that flags anomalous role assignments; 2) audit prompt templates to ensure control tokens are unforgeable; 3) train models with adversarial examples that mix fake structure and content to harden against spoofing attacks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a security issue relevant to LLM-based agents and APIs used in enterprise settings, giving a moderate real-world impact. The solutions are largely experimental and not yet deployed, so maturity is low. However, the detection method could be packaged as a security service for SaaS or cloud platforms within a short time, giving a moderate monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Request-Adaptive Execution for Efficient Hybrid LLM Inference
case_studies.abstract: Hybrid large language models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising way to combine the modeling capability of the Attention mechanism with the efficiency of state space models (SSMs). However, most existing hybrid LLMs still inherit a static design philosophy: once the Attention-to-SSM layout is chosen, every request must follow the same hybrid execution. This one-layout-fits-all design is inefficient for real-world serving workloads, where different requests rely on contextual information in different ways. This paper presents Morph, a serving system that co-designs the model architecture and runtime for request-adaptive hybrid LLM inference. Its model architecture pairs Attention and SSM layers within each block and uses prefill-oriented gating to select a request-specific layout that remains fixed throughout decoding. Its serving runtime preserves batching efficiency under divergent layer choices through selective batching and enables correct prefix reuse through hybrid-aware context caching. Experiments on six datasets show that Morph achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than existing static hybrid baselines. System-level evaluation further shows that Morph improves the serving throughput by up to 3.87x over baselines while substantially reducing inference latency.
case_studies.summary: Morph lets cloud services adapt the mix of Attention and State Space Model layers to each request, cutting inference time and boosting throughput by up to 3.87×. The system re‑architects the model and runtime to choose a fixed, request‑specific layout and batch similar calls together, while re‑using context where possible.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference, step 1: profile your request mix to see if different queries need different layer mixes. Step 2: adopt a hybrid model with pre‑fill gating and a runtime that selectively batches similar layouts. Step 3: enable hybrid‑aware context caching to keep latency low while maintaining high throughput.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes Morph, a request-adaptive hybrid LLM inference serving system that directly targets performance and efficiency in real-world LLM deployment scenarios. It offers concrete architectural and runtime innovations that can be integrated into existing AI infrastructure, making it highly relevant to IT engineers managing LLM workloads. The system appears to be built and tested, with released code or a working prototype, indicating moderate maturity. It presents actionable techniques that can be adopted or sold as a service within 90 days, such as improving throughput and reducing latency for LLM-based APIs, thus providing clear monetization potential. Overall, the paper scores strongly across all three criteria.

case_studies.title: From Ripple to Boundary: Deterministic Impact Boundaries for LLM-Based Software Evolution
case_studies.abstract: The landscape of software evolution is undergoing a fundamental paradigm shift in the era of Large Language Models. As industrial software engineering increasingly transitions toward design-driven code generation, the bottleneck of evolution has shifted from writing code to maintaining deterministic consistency between multi-source design assets and the generated code. When a design asset changes, LLM agents currently lack a deterministic impact boundary to identify which code must be evolved, leading to two failure modes: hallucinating missing changes or breaking unrelated code. Probabilistic approaches, such as semantic retrieval or text-based diffing, fail to capture the structural ripple effects across highly interconnected design dependencies. We propose a paradigm shift from probabilistic semantic retrieval to deterministic structural constraints. We formalize the design assets as a Knowledge Graph and organize them into a content-addressed Merkle Directed Acyclic Graph. Our key insight reveals a topological isomorphism between the logical ripple effect of a design change and the content hash propagation within the DAG. By leveraging this, we transform ambiguous impact analysis into verifiable structural operations. Through a two-phase diffing process, we extract a precise causal chain that defines the exact modification boundary. This boundary enables deterministic context injection, providing the LLM agent with strictly scoped code and design updates, thereby fundamentally guaranteeing evolution safety. As a by-product, the KG serves as an agent-queryable knowledge base for natural language design retrieval. Early deployment on a large-scale industrial payment platform demonstrates that our mechanism successfully computes the exact impact boundary and generates incremental code modifications that meet the expected design changes.
case_studies.summary: The paper tackles the problem of reliably determining which parts of code need to change when a design asset is updated in a system that uses large language models for code generation. It builds a knowledge‑graph based Merkle DAG that maps design assets to code, allowing a deterministic calculation of the exact impact boundary for any change. The result is an automated, verifiable process that can safely produce incremental code modifications and avoid unintended side effects. This is directly relevant for cloud infrastructure managers who use LLM‑based tools for configuration or IaC generation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑driven cloud infra, here is what to do: 1) model your IaC templates and design docs as a knowledge graph, 2) construct a Merkle‑DAG over that graph to capture hash propagation, 3) use the deterministic boundary to inject only the affected code into the LLM for incremental updates, ensuring consistency and safety.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses deterministic impact boundaries for LLM-generated code, directly affecting software evolution workflows. It reports early deployment on an industrial payment platform, indicating a working system but not a mature, widely released product. The approach could be packaged as a service or tool for IT engineers within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
case_studies.abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.
case_studies.summary: OpenClaw, an AI assistant platform, suffers from widespread security gaps—especially in access control, data leaks, and injection attacks—found in 521 CWE instances across 59 types. The study maps these weaknesses to the agent’s trust boundaries and offers seven mitigation tactics, showing that unsafe tool use and execution containment are major risks.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage OpenClaw or similar agentic systems, set explicit trust boundaries for user input, enforce least‑privilege access for tools, sandbox local execution, and monitor runtime behaviour to catch injection or data‑leak attempts.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on security vulnerabilities in agentic AI systems, directly relevant to IT engineers managing secure deployments. It provides empirical findings and mitigation strategies, indicating a mature but not production-ready solution, thus moderate maturity. Monetisation potential is limited to advisory services or internal tooling improvements, offering modest commercial value.

case_studies.title: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
case_studies.abstract: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, and established it as a defense surface independent of the LLM layer and the agent layer; however, that work only tested the envelope layer briefly and did not examine how label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffold differences, or existing memories affect defense effectiveness. Following its GDA Measurement methodology and the A/B/C/D outcome taxonomy, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle, uses the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator with the semantic refusal rate as its complementary reference, and characterizes the security boundary of the envelope layer through a two-by-two factorial experiment and a memory experiment. The results show that: when the envelope is authentic, strong labels consistently reduce the semantic breach rate, whereas weak labels are not necessarily better than an unlabeled baseline; when the envelope can be forged, the benefit of strong labels is weakened and its direction varies across frontends; and memory has a larger effect than any label manipulation: success memory raises the semantic breach rate while failure memory lowers it, and most combinations that contain both experiences return to the no-memory baseline. Accordingly, this paper refines the envelope layer from a single admission channel into two levels, an admission channel plus a context assembly surface, and argues that its security boundary is not a fixed property of labels but a dynamic outcome jointly shaped by label claims, frontend permissions, and historical memory.
case_studies.summary: This paper shows that how we label and authenticate inputs to an LLM agent – the so‑called envelope layer – can drastically change how often the agent slips into unwanted behaviour. By testing different label strengths, authenticity, and the agent’s past memory, they found that strong labels lower the risk only when the envelope is authentic, and that the agent’s memory can swing risk up or down more than any label tweak. The work suggests that the envelope is not a fixed defence but a dynamic surface that changes with context.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLM services, first audit the input‑validation pipeline to ensure each request carries an authentic, strong label; second, monitor the agent’s memory logs for recent successful or failed interactions and adjust the refusal thresholds accordingly; third, implement a separate context‑assembly layer that re‑evaluates content based on both label strength and memory state before it reaches the model.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents experimental results on a security layer for LLM agents, offering insights that could inform defensive practices for AI systems. However, it lacks a ready-to-deploy implementation and is limited to research experiments. While the findings could guide future engineering, immediate commercial application within 90 days is unlikely. Thus, scores are modest across all dimensions.

case_studies.title: Built to Remember, Shipped to Forget: Operational Contracts, Failures, and Repairs in Containerized LLM Agent Deployments
case_studies.abstract: LLM agent systems reach production as container images run by platforms such as Docker, Compose, and Kubernetes. Framework and platform document opposite expectations: to the platform a container is disposable, while the framework persists conversations, pauses runs for human input, and resumes interrupted work from saved state; each side specifies only its own behavior, so the obligations their composition creates are stated nowhere. We present the first empirical study of this boundary, stating these obligations as operational contracts: guarantees a deployment must provide to preserve an agent system's required behavior when a deployment-platform event occurs. From the first-party documentation of LangGraph and the three platforms we derive 14 contracts and evaluate them with three independent sources of evidence: 433 deployed open-source agent systems, seven events induced on 12 of them, and 122 developer repairs mined from 39,261 commits, pull requests, and issues. At least one contract applies to 75.5% of the systems, yet its guarantee is routinely missing: of systems that must keep state beyond the process, 37.4% lose it to a restart and 41.5% to a container replacement, and every assessable deployment stops the framework's production server mid-drain. Induced events turn 14 of 16 predicted violations into runtime failures and all seven predicted holds pass. The failures are born in deployment but repaired in code: developer repairs independently cover twelve of the fourteen contracts, 78% change application code, and only two in three fully restore the violated guarantee. The 14-contract catalogue, detection rules, fault-injection harness, and 35-pattern repair taxonomy provide a basis for checking and strengthening agent deployments.
case_studies.summary: This study maps 14 operational contracts that must hold when running LLM agent containers on Docker, Compose or Kubernetes, and shows that many deployments miss these guarantees, causing state loss and failures. The authors provide a catalogue, detection rules, a fault‑injection tool and a taxonomy of 35 repair patterns to help detect and fix such issues. For most IT infrastructure teams, the findings are highly relevant because they expose hidden dependencies between container lifecycle events and agent state management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage containerised LLM agents, check your platform and framework documentation for the 14 contracts; use the supplied detection rules to scan your deployments for missing guarantees; and apply the 35 repair patterns to fix state‑loss or interruption failures before they hit production.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses operational contracts for containerized LLM agent deployments, directly impacting how IT engineers manage state persistence, failure handling, and deployment practices in Kubernetes/Docker environments. It provides empirical evidence, a contract catalogue, detection rules, and repair patterns that can be adopted or adapted by practitioners. While the research is mature (published with empirical data and tooling), it is still an academic study rather than a ready-to-deploy product, so the maturity score reflects that. The monetisation potential is moderate: engineers could incorporate these contracts and repair patterns into their CI/CD pipelines or offer consulting services on agent deployment reliability, but it is not an off-the-shelf SaaS offering. Thus the total score is 55 out of 75.

case_studies.title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
case_studies.abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the issue of keeping autonomous robots’ self‑developed goals aligned with human intentions. The authors built a multimodal system that uses large language and vision models to turn natural‑language user goals into robot missions and drives, then tests it in simulation and on a real robot, showing that the robots produce valid, aligned behaviours.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on aligning autonomous robots using LLMs and VLMs, which is outside the typical IT infrastructure concerns of the target audience. The system is demonstrated in simulation and a single physical robot, indicating limited practical deployment. No evidence of released code or scalable tooling that an IT engineer could adopt or sell within 90 days. Thus, the impact, maturity, and monetisation potential are modest.

case_studies.title: AgentProofBench: Benchmarking Reusable Verifiers for Web Agents
case_studies.abstract: Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow changing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen acceptance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48 families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse-rebuild BA intervals are [-5.47, 1.57] and [-10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22 execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11 with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continuation attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution consequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable at both the requirement and policy levels.
case_studies.summary: AgentProofBench provides a benchmark for reusable verification of web agents, linking acceptance rules to execution outcomes across many tasks and services. It builds a dataset of 97 tasks, 79 families, and four web services, and shows that reusable verification can maintain high correctness rates. The study offers a concrete baseline for measuring verification quality, which is relevant for managing cloud‑based AI services.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for AI services, use AgentProofBench to test your verification rules against real execution scenarios: 1) Run the benchmark tests to evaluate your rule compliance; 2) Compare your system’s success rates to the reported 82/96 and 79/96 scores; 3) Adjust your verification logic if your rates fall below the baseline to improve reliability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a benchmark for verifying web agents, which is a niche area with limited direct impact on current IT infrastructure workflows. The methodology and datasets are available, indicating some maturity, but it is primarily a research benchmark rather than a deployable system. There is no clear immediate commercial application that an IT engineer could adopt or sell within 90 days.

case_studies.title: Agentic AI Orchestration Framework for Spatial Intelligence: Supply Chain Deployment
case_studies.abstract: Industrial spatial decisions are assembled across systems that share neither a reference frame nor an owner, and analysts spend substantial effort reconciling those systems rather than reasoning about space. This paper presents ANASSA, a reference architecture integrating structured reasoning, multi-agent workflow orchestration, authoritative spatial grounding, and feedback-driven execution, and reports its instantiation in an operating supply-chain deployment. The architecture places typed data contracts at agent boundaries, validates spatial claims against a certified authoritative foundation, and enforces two blocking human-in-the-loop approvals inside a six-step cognitive loop. The deployment covers multi-hazard risk assessment on an ocean-and-inland freight lane, including cold-chain excursion detection over container telemetry.
